line: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 c3 Nf6 e5
teaches: A central pawn push made before you can support it just loses time. When the advance can be met by a clean capture that leaves you ahead in development, welcome it — the space it grabbed evaporates and you are simply better for having let it come.
explains: The pawn on e5 attacks the knight on f6, but the advance is premature: the pawn on c3 sits idle and the e5-pawn itself is loose, so capturing it leaves Black a tempo ahead in development.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 c3 Nf6 e5 dxe5 Nxe5 Nbd7
teaches: Meet a centralised enemy knight by challenging it with a developing move that offers a trade on your terms. Bringing a piece out while forcing the exchange is far better than tolerating the knight in your camp.
explains: The knight comes to d7, developing and attacking the knight on e5 to offer a trade. Whatever White does, Black emerges comfortably developed and a shade better.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 c3 Nf6 e5 dxe5 Nxe5 Nbd7 Nxd7 Bxd7
teaches: When you recapture, do it with the piece that also develops — a recapture that brings a man toward activity is two moves in one. Prefer the take that improves your position over the passive one.
explains: Taking back with the bishop develops it and sets up a reroute to c6 on the long diagonal, rather than recapturing passively with the queen. The recapture is also a developing move.

line: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 c3 Nf6 e5 dxe5 Nxe5 Nbd7 Nxd7 Bxd7 Bc4 Bc6
teaches: An awkwardly placed bishop should be rerouted to its best diagonal, and doing it with a gain of tempo forces the opponent to react before you finish your own plan. Move the bad piece to a good square while attacking something.
explains: The bishop swings to c6, seizing the long diagonal and attacking the g2-pawn, which forces White to respond before Black calmly completes with e6, the dark-squared bishop and castling.
